mcqs.q: Endodontics is derived from words meaning:
mcqs.explain: Endo = inside, odont = tooth; the study of the pulp and periradicular tissues.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of pulpal/periradicular disease is:
mcqs.explain: Pulp/periradicular pathosis is primarily a microbial disease, most often initiated by caries.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of endodontic treatment?
mcqs.explain: Access opening → cleaning & shaping → obturation → (coronal-seal) restoration.

mcqs.q: Before starting root canal treatment, the clinician should ensure that:
opts: A restorative (final restoration) plan has been approved
The tooth is definitely going to be extracted
mcqs.explain: The final restoration provides the coronal seal and is a continuum of RCT — its plan must be approved beforehand.

mcqs.q: Which is a CONTRAINDICATION to endodontic treatment?
opts: A vertical root fracture / non-restorable tooth
An apical abscess on a restorable tooth
mcqs.explain: Non-restorable teeth (VRF, deep crack, poor crown:root, severe resorption), uncooperative patients and non-strategic teeth are contraindications.

mcqs.q: Rubber dam application in the steps of RCT is done:
mcqs.explain: Order: assessment → diagnosis/plan → rubber dam → access → working length → clean & shape → obturate → coronal seal.

mcqs.q: Placing a material directly on a mechanical/traumatic vital pulp exposure is a:
mcqs.explain: Direct pulp cap = material (Ca(OH)₂/MTA) directly on an exposed vital pulp; indirect cap is over remaining caries without exposure.

mcqs.q: Removal of only the coronal portion of a vital pulp, preserving the radicular pulp, is a:
mcqs.explain: Pulpotomy removes the coronal pulp and keeps the radicular pulp vital (e.g. Cvek pulpotomy after trauma).

mcqs.q: Apexogenesis differs from apexification in that apexogenesis:
opts: Encourages continued root-end development in a VITAL tooth
Induces a calcified barrier in a NON-vital open apex
mcqs.explain: Apexogenesis = continued root development in a vital tooth; apexification = a calcified barrier in a non-vital tooth with an open apex.

mcqs.q: Agents commonly used for internal bleaching of an endodontically treated tooth are:
opts: Sodium perborate and hydrogen peroxide (or saline)
mcqs.explain: Internal bleaching uses oxidizing agents — sodium perborate with hydrogen peroxide or saline.

mcqs.q: In Fish's zones of inflammation, the zone containing polymorphs and microbes is the zone of:
mcqs.explain: Zone of infection = polymorphs + microbes; contamination has no bacteria; irritation has macrophages/osteoclasts; stimulation has fibroblasts/osteoblasts.

saqs.q: Define endodontics and state the main objective of endodontic therapy.
saqs.a: Endodontics (endo = inside, odont = tooth) is the study and practice concerned with the biology of the pulp and the etiology, diagnosis, prevention and treatment of diseases/injuries of the pulp and associated periradicular tissues. The main objective is thorough shaping and cleaning of all pulp spaces followed by complete obturation with an inert filling material.

saqs.q: State the phases of endodontic treatment and why the final restoration matters.
saqs.a: The four phases are: 1) access opening, 2) cleaning and shaping, 3) obturation, and 4) restoration. The final restoration provides the coronal seal that protects tooth structure and prevents coronal microleakage, so it is a continuum of RCT and its plan must be approved before treatment begins.

saqs.q: Give three indications and three contraindications for endodontic treatment.
saqs.a: Indications (any 3): irreversibly inflamed or necrotic pulp; apical periodontitis or abscess; prosthetic/intentional endodontics; after certain traumatic injuries; prophylactic/elective. Contraindications (any 3): non-restorable teeth (inadequate periodontal support, vertical root fracture, deep crack, poor crown:root ratio, insufficient tooth structure, severe resorption); uncooperative patient or refusal; unimprovable poor oral condition; non-strategic tooth.

saqs.q: Name and briefly describe Fish's four zones of inflammation.
saqs.a: 1) Zone of infection — polymorphs and microbes. 2) Zone of contamination — round-cell infiltration, cellular destruction, dead bone cells and lymphocytes, but no bacteria. 3) Zone of irritation — macrophages and osteoclasts, with collagen digested by phagocytic cells and normal bone cells. 4) Zone of stimulation — fibroblasts and osteoblasts, where the toxin acts as a stimulant and collagen forms a defensive wall and scaffold for new bone.
